figures.title: Equation-family decision map
figures.description: Depict the foundation problem exactly: Solve sqrt(x+1)=x-1. Show the quantities, axes, intervals, or algebraic objects needed to reach this conclusion: The domain requires x≥1. Squaring gives candidates 0 and 3; only x=3 checks.
figures.anchorConclusion: The domain requires x≥1. Squaring gives candidates 0 and 3; only x=3 checks.
figures.anchorInterpretation: Squaring can enlarge the candidate set.
figures.mechanism: Classify the family, state restrictions, use reversible steps when possible, label candidate-generating steps such as squaring or denominator clearing, and check candidates in the original statement.
figures.validStructure: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the order. Rational, radical, logarithmic, and even-power steps require domain checks.
figures.invalidMove: A frequent error is reporting every algebraic candidate as a solution without checking the original equation.
figures.lessonOutcome: Classify and solve common equation and inequality families while distinguishing reversible steps from candidate-generating steps.

figures.title: Factoring decision sequence
figures.description: Depict the foundation problem exactly: Factor x^4-5x^2+4. Show the quantities, axes, intervals, or algebraic objects needed to reach this conclusion: Let u=x^2. Then (u-1)(u-4), so (x-1)(x+1)(x-2)(x+2).
figures.anchorInterpretation: Repeated powers can hide familiar quadratic structure.
figures.mechanism: Extract a greatest common factor first, recognize grouping or special-product structure, factor each result again, and verify by multiplication.
figures.validStructure: A factorization is complete only over the stated coefficient system. Repeated powers may hide a quadratic-in-form pattern.
figures.invalidMove: A frequent error is stopping after one factorization step or cancelling terms that are not common factors.
figures.lessonOutcome: Recognize and apply the principal factoring structures needed for polynomial-function analysis.

figures.title: Legal versus illegal cancellation
figures.description: Depict the foundation problem exactly: Simplify (x^2+x-6)/(x^2-4). Show the quantities, axes, intervals, or algebraic objects needed to reach this conclusion: The result is (x+3)/(x+2), with x≠2,-2.
figures.anchorInterpretation: The cancelled factor at x=2 remains an exclusion.
figures.mechanism: Record restrictions, factor completely, cancel only common factors, combine over a least common denominator, and check equation candidates against the original domain.
figures.validStructure: A divisor rational expression must be nonzero. Cancellation is division by a common factor, not removal of matching terms across addition.
figures.invalidMove: A frequent error is erasing the original restriction after cancellation.
figures.lessonOutcome: Simplify and solve rational expressions while preserving every restriction from the original form.

figures.title: Principal root versus equation roots
figures.description: Depict the foundation problem exactly: Solve sqrt(x+6)=x. Show the quantities, axes, intervals, or algebraic objects needed to reach this conclusion: Candidates are 3 and -2; only x=3 satisfies the original equation.
figures.anchorConclusion: Candidates are 3 and -2; only x=3 satisfies the original equation.
figures.anchorInterpretation: The domain removes the extraneous value.
figures.mechanism: Extract perfect powers, convert between radical and rational-exponent notation, isolate a radical in an equation, raise both sides to a power, and check every candidate.
figures.validStructure: Negative rational exponents also require a nonzero base. Squaring is not reversible without sign and domain checks.
figures.invalidMove: A frequent error is replacing sqrt(x^2) with x for negative inputs or omitting the final check.
figures.lessonOutcome: Move among radical and rational-exponent forms, simplify exact values, and reject extraneous candidates.

figures.title: Exponent-law derivation
figures.description: Depict the foundation problem exactly: Evaluate log_3(1/27). Show the quantities, axes, intervals, or algebraic objects needed to reach this conclusion: -3, because 3^(-3)=1/27.
figures.anchorInterpretation: A logarithm reports an exponent.
figures.mechanism: Apply product, quotient, and power laws only to multiplicative structure; convert log_b(y)=x and b^x=y without changing the base-exponent-output roles.
figures.validStructure: Real logarithm arguments must be positive, and bases must be positive and unequal to 1.
figures.invalidMove: A frequent error is applying a product law to a sum, such as log(a+b)=log a+log b.
figures.lessonOutcome: Apply exponent and logarithm laws, convert between inverse forms, and solve basic equations with valid domains.
